Series::leaky_relu¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::leaky_relu(double negative_slope) const -> Series
Series& Series::leaky_relu_(double negative_slope)

What It Does¶

leaky_relu() is relu() with a small non-zero slope on the negative side:

leaky_relu(x) = x            if x >= 0
              = slope * x    if x < 0

relu() zeroes every negative input, and a unit that outputs 0 also has gradient 0, so it can get stuck (“die”) and never recover. leaky_relu() lets a small fraction of the negative signal — and its gradient — through, so the unit keeps learning.

Typical negative_slope values are 0.01 or 0.1. The slope is a fixed hyperparameter here; for a learned per-channel slope use prelu().

An integer input is promoted to a floating-point result, since a fractional slope produces non-integers.

Parameters¶

negative_slope (double)

The multiplier applied to negative inputs. Required (there is no default).

Returns¶

Series or Series& The activated values. leaky_relu_() overwrites the current storage.

Gradient¶

leaky_relu() is differentiable:

d/dx leaky_relu(x) = 1      if x >= 0
                   = slope  if x < 0

The boundary at x = 0 takes the >= 0 branch, so its gradient is 1. Unlike relu(), the negative-side gradient is slope rather than 0.

Examples¶

Example 1. A 0.1 slope on the negative half, identity on the positive half.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 3.0}).leaky_relu(0.1));

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.3000, -0.1000, 0.0000, 1.0000, 3.0000]

Example 2. A smaller slope leaks less.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 3.0}).leaky_relu(0.01));

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.0300, -0.0100, 0.0000, 1.0000, 3.0000]

Example 3. The backward is 1 on the non-negative side and slope on the negative side.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

x.leaky_relu(0.1).sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[0.1000, 0.1000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000]

The negative positions keep a 0.1 gradient — the whole point of the “leak”.

Example 4. An integer input is promoted rather than truncating the slope.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-2, -1, 0, 3}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64).leaky_relu(0.1));

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.2000, -0.1000, 0.0000, 3.0000]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • negative_slope has no default; you must pass it.

  • The gradient at exactly x = 0 is 1 (the non-negative branch).

  • For a learned slope, use prelu(); leaky_relu()’s slope is a fixed constant.

Summary¶

leaky_relu(x, slope) is relu() with a leak:

  • x for x >= 0, slope * x for x < 0

  • promotes integer input to floating point

  • differentiable: gradient 1 on the non-negative side, slope on the negative side

See Also¶

  • Series::relu: the slope = 0 case, prone to dying units.

  • Series::prelu: the same shape with a learnable slope.

  • Series::gelu / Series::silu: smooth alternatives.
